routing_warnings.description: This message specifies how the 5V and 3V3 rails enter and leave the main board, so it primarily concerns board-chain power distribution rather than changing the connector interface.
This message defines the sensor-board input and module-connector topology, which has a narrower existing Requirement.
This message adds a panel-button connector tapping PWRON; it concerns panel power control rather than modifying the interboard connector itself.
The distinct new detail is the INA219 series path and downstream 3.3V measurement; the board-chain forwarding behavior already appears in messages 343 and 347.

The inability to fit the connectors within the 68 mm board constraint is a general power-board mechanical-layout issue; the resulting battery-specific placement change is captured separately at message 77.
The J_BAT short-edge constraint applies to the later single integrated board rather than the power-board battery interface.
The battery-connector accessibility concern concerns the later integrated board and its enclosure-facing USB-C placement.
The successful USB workaround concerns the later integrated board's native USB path, not the power-board USB connector requirement.
The message concerns acceptance of the USB connector's footprint openings rather than the power board's overall mechanical layout.
The DCDC1 3.4V setpoint clause concerns the separate power-board output-setpoint Requirement rather than core AXP2101 topology.
The decision to retain AXP2101 concerns the later integrated-board power-management architecture.
The request to expose PWROK and VBACKUP belongs to the integrated-board auxiliary-pin Requirement.
The contiguous pours and stitching-via requirements concern integrated-board high-current routing.
The manufactured-board L3 voltage instability concerns integrated-board DCDC1 regulation and load stability, not the earlier power-board topology Requirement.
The unsuccessful AXP2101 replacement concerns integrated-board assembly reliability.
This message defines when the main board uses its standalone LDO versus power-board DCDC1; it does not change the power-board DCDC1 output setpoint.
The L3 voltage observations concern manufactured integrated-board DCDC1 regulation rather than the earlier power-board setpoint requirement.
This duplicates the integrated-board L3 regulation outcome and does not test the separate power-board setpoint requirement.
The detailed DCDC1 undervoltage, transient-collapse, and 3.4V programming results concern the later single integrated board.
The unsuccessful AXP2101 replacement concerns the integrated board's suspected device or assembly reliability, not the power-board setpoint.
The grounded USBLC6 VBUS pin concerns native USB operation on the later integrated board, not the main-board standalone LDO supply.
The requested USB ESD-symbol correction belongs to the integrated board's native USB interface.
The requested 3.4V DCDC1 setpoint compensates for the OR-ing diode drop but directly changes the power-board DCDC1 output Requirement.
Placement of the INA219 immediately after the Schottky diodes specifies the current-monitoring path rather than changing the OR-ing behavior.
The GPIO20 and GPIO19 USB routing observation concerns the later integrated board's native USB interface, not the separate main-board GPIO mapping.
This message adds a panel-mounted power-button connector carrying PWRON, which belongs to the separate panel power-control Requirement.
This message reviews pull-resistor behavior for buttons and a slide switch on the later integrated single-board design.
This correction to the button and switch pull resistors applies to the later integrated-board input circuit.
The reported inability to fit the connectors and components is a board-layout failure rather than evidence that the connector inventory itself is incorrect.
The missing JLCPCB components concern parts availability rather than omission from the main-board design.
The two connectors marked missing in JLCPCB's parts list concern production-package population and sourcing, while later context says the connectors are present in the design.
The client's willingness to proceed without the unavailable connector parts concerns assembly population, not removal from the design inventory.
The request to add the connectors follows a BOM and parts-list discussion and is better routed as an assembly-population requirement.
The additional I2C connector is for the later integrated board, not the separate main board.
The omitted JST-GH connector belongs to the later integrated-board connector set.
Cable length, bus speed, and shared pull-up value concern the bus-level electrical Requirement rather than main-board series-resistor topology.
Moving the shared I2C pull-ups to the main board concerns bus-level pull-up placement rather than the series-resistor topology.
The conditional approval verifies the 4.4kΩ pull-ups, not the optional 44Ω series resistors or their topology.
This failure explicitly concerns the sensor board having a layout problem similar to the main board.
The immediately preceding exchange concerns whether the sensor-board arrangement fits, so this placement claim should not be assigned to the main-board layout.
The client discusses omitting the physical connectors beside the ESP32 while retaining their holes, which concerns the full-pin breakout rather than general board layout.
This orientation decision concerns the later single integrated board and its enclosure.
This delegates orientation selection for the later integrated board, not the earlier main board.
The accepted connector-access revision concerns the later integrated-board mechanical layout.
This pin-header pitch discussion concerns the later integrated-board design; the client explicitly distinguishes it from the earlier separate main board.
The MOSFET arrangement for switching the positive 3.3V load rail is owned by the narrower switched-load circuit Requirement.
The reported 3.3V/data pin mismatch concerns the separate LED-board connector pinout rather than the main-board LED supply and logic design.
This message governs top-edge placement and alignment of the sensor-board connectors rather than their electrical topology or inventory.
The reported sensor-board problem concerns component or connector placement and is followed by a proposed orientation change.
The incorrect sensor-board BOM is a production-package failure, not a change to the connector topology.
The requested Gerbers, drill files, positions file, and corrected BOM belong to the sensor-board production package.
The required connectors are missing from the sourcing or manufacturing setup, while the sensor-board design itself already contains the connector topology.
The reported inability to fit everything explicitly concerns the supplied main-board dimensions.
The insufficient-space observation continues the main-board layout discussion rather than describing the sensor board.
The component-and-connector fit failure occurs within the ongoing main-board resizing discussion.
The client's conclusion that the required layout is impossible at the current size concerns the main board.
The 140×100 resize, connector retention, and ESP32 edge placement apply to the main-board layout.
The bottom-edge connector reorientation remains part of the preceding main-board layout exchange.
This message defines battery-charge status indication through the LED chain rather than the LED array's model, count, package, or spacing.
This message concerns LED supply voltage and logic-level shifting rather than the physical LED array.
The possible removal of the level shifter concerns LED power and logic handling, not array composition.
The change from 5V to 3.3V and removal of the level shifter concern LED power and logic handling.
The reported 3.3V/data-pin swap concerns the LED-board connector pinout, not the LED array.
The observed connection of LED pin 1 to 3.3V verifies the pinout concern rather than array composition.
The completion statement resolves the immediately preceding pinout review and does not concretely verify the array's count, package, or spacing.

The concern about Extended-tier setup fees and alternative basic-tier parts primarily concerns component sourceability and manufacturing cost rather than completeness of the power-board production package.
The wrong BOM identified in the sensor-board folder belongs to the sensor-board production package.
The requested Gerbers, NPTH and PTH drill files, positions file, and corrected BOM are explicitly for the sensor board.
The manufacturing workflow still reporting two missing components concerns component availability or substitution, not the power-board production-file package.
The client states that the two connectors can be omitted; this changes physical connector population rather than independently establishing a production-package correction.

The generic statement that the zip contains every required file immediately follows the client's question about the power-board file, so it should not be treated as a sensor-board implementation claim.
The missing machine-local 3D model files concern portable KiCad project libraries rather than completeness of the manufacturing package.
The decision to split power and signal connectors changes the interboard interface topology rather than the general sourceability constraint.
Acceptance of ordering the sensor board in its current configuration and optionally including inexpensive connectors concerns the sensor-board order package.
The preference for JLCPCB Basic components in the new single-board design is primarily an integrated-board cost-optimization requirement.
The client's request to find a lower-cost connector alternative primarily changes the component-sourceability requirement; only the resulting cart update pertains to the target requirement.
Reducing connector count is a cost-optimization detail rather than a separate change to the established single-board architecture.
The possible removal of items to simplify the design concerns cost and design simplification; it does not establish a definite architecture change.
The accepted flexibility in connector placement concerns the integrated board's mechanical layout rather than its single-board architecture.
The decision to use through-hole connectors throughout belongs to the independent connector-assembly requirement rather than the general cost-optimization requirement.
The requested additional I2C JST connector is specifically for the display light sensor and is better routed to the narrower light-sensor-port Requirement.
The revised specification specifically incorporates the light-sensor I2C connector rather than changing the general peripheral-connector set.
The instruction to use through-hole connectors throughout changes connector assembly technology, not connector-set completeness.
The button pull-up and PIR/touch pull-down clauses concern the integrated-board input-biasing Requirement rather than the auxiliary AXP2101 pins.
The reported R16/R17/R18 implementation belongs to the integrated-board button-input Requirement.
The observed absence of voltage at sensor pins concerns integrated-board power delivery behavior and does not specifically establish a high-current copper-routing failure.
The fluctuating L3 output is runtime evidence for DCDC1 regulation and load stability rather than high-current trace capacity.
The persistent failure after replacing AXP2101 belongs to the DCDC1 regulation trajectory and does not identify high-current routing as the cause.
The suspected thermal-pad soldering and full paste-aperture yield issue concerns AXP2101 assembly reliability in addition to the observed DCDC1 regulation failure.
The concrete failure in this message is native USB non-enumeration; the successful idle 3.3V observation does not verify DCDC1 load stability.
The source also reports concrete post-rework verification that native USB enumerates and supports flashing.
The requirement to keep components in place during a drop concerns mounting and retention rather than enclosure capacity.
Grouping the display connectors on the edge nearest the display-flex route constrains the integrated PCB connector layout rather than the enclosure display mount or cover cutout.
The accepted addition of NTC sensing to J_BAT belongs to the separate battery-temperature-monitoring Requirement; only the battery-protection behavior is retained here.
The three-pin JST-PH pinout, including its NTC pin, changes the physical battery interface rather than independently changing the temperature-monitoring behavior.
This placement request concerns ESP32 decoupling on the later single integrated board, not the earlier main board.
This message concerns AXP2101 and MT3608 decoupling placement on the integrated board.
The assessment that the ESP32 capacitors can remain unchanged addresses the integrated-board ESP32 decoupling discussion.
The client's instruction to leave the capacitors unchanged resolves the integrated-board ESP32 decoupling request.
This message concerns AXP2101 and MT3608 local decoupling rather than ESP32-module decoupling.
The local-input-decoupling question concerns the AXP2101 DCDC1 VIN pins, not the ESP32 decoupling network.
In context, the freelancer's capacitor check addresses the AXP2101 DCDC1 input decoupling.
The capacitors beside the USB connector are converter-input decoupling and do not describe ESP32 local decoupling.

The observed low output, load-transient rail collapse, and DCDC1 failure are runtime evidence for DCDC1 regulation. The message mentions local VIN decoupling only as an unconfirmed diagnostic hypothesis and does not establish a decoupling failure.
The request for three missing 3D-model files primarily concerns bundling project assets; the later message 934 provides the more direct evidence for portable reference paths.
The statement that every library should have been included concerns missing bundled project assets rather than the portability of their reference paths.
The USBLC6 library defect incorrectly joining GND and VBUS is an electrical USB-protection issue, not a KiCad path-portability issue.
The possible KiCad-version incompatibility concerns portable project references rather than delivery of the three missing 3D model files.
The footprint being unavailable in the client's KiCad installation concerns library and version compatibility rather than bundled 3D assets.
This message primarily reports absolute-path failures and their replacement with cross-machine relative paths.
The KiCad 8 versus KiCad 9 third-party variable mismatch is a project-reference portability issue.
The statement specifically establishes operation without a battery, for which the inventory contains a narrower Requirement.
The AXP specification check concerns the narrower no-battery operating behavior and is not runtime verification of the overall power-management architecture.
The observed L3 voltage instability and partial manufacturing yield directly concern DCDC1 regulation.
The concrete failure reported here is native USB enumeration; the brief successful rail startup does not verify the complete power-management Requirement.
The suspected USBLC6 VBUS wiring error concerns the narrower USB ESD-protection Requirement.
The rail-collapse, low regulation, transient instability, and DCDC1 deterioration form a distinct execution trajectory for the narrower DCDC1 regulation Requirement.
The unsuccessful AXP2101 replacement is follow-up evidence in the persistent DCDC1 failure investigation, not a change to the selected power-management architecture.
The concrete failure in this message is native USB enumeration across the integrated-board samples; the power observation does not establish full no-battery operation.
Removing U3 and joining the USB data lines verifies native USB operation rather than no-battery power behavior.
The same source also contains a distinct DCDC1 setpoint and load-stability failure that should be represented under the DCDC1 regulation Requirement.
The identified USBLC6 pin-5 miswiring is specifically an ESD-protection circuit defect; it explains the native-USB failure but is better represented under the separate USB ESD protection Requirement.
The requested correction of USBLC6 VBUS, GND, and D+/D- pass-through wiring directly modifies the separate USB ESD protection Requirement.
The failure to enumerate in normal and forced-download modes is direct runtime evidence for native USB operation; it is only supporting context for the ESD-protection wiring failure.
Successful USB operation after removing U3 and bridging the data lines verifies the native USB path, not ESD protection, because the workaround leaves ESD protection absent.
The PIR and touch pull-down configuration is an independently identified input-biasing Requirement and should not be included in the button and switch lifecycle.
The VRTC, VBACKUP, and PWROK decisions belong to the AXP2101 auxiliary-pin Requirement.
The VBACKUP header and VRTC output portions of this completion claim belong to the AXP2101 auxiliary-pin Requirement.

missing_requirement_candidates.description: These messages independently establish and diagnose USBLC6-based ESD protection on the later integrated board. USB can operate after bypassing the component while ESD protection remains absent, so this behavior is distinct from the power-board TVS requirement and from basic native-USB operation.
The client independently requires an easy-to-assemble case, a behavior not fully represented by component capacity, display installation, or drop retention.

The client independently requires the overall case to be easy to assemble; this is distinct from component mounting and drop retention and is not fully represented by an existing enclosure Requirement.
